title: The Real Threat of AI Is Not Unemployment, But Stagnant Wages

content_html:
A new white paper released by Apollo Global Management presents an counterintuitive conclusion: AI may not directly take people's jobs, but it could first depress wages. A study tracking wage and employment data across 321 occupations shows that since 2023—roughly coinciding with the rapid rise of ChatGPT—the average wage growth for jobs with the highest AI exposure fell by 6.7%.

The research has not yet found a "detectable" impact of AI on overall employment, meaning that more people are currently facing the reality of difficulty in getting raises rather than anxiety about unemployment.

Low-income groups are hit first, and programmers are also not immune

The distribution of wage impacts is highly uneven. Since 2023, the income growth of service workers has averaged a decline of 24.3%, and the income of those in the bottom 25% dropped by 10.7%, while the highest-income group experienced no "significant impact." Researchers also used the Anthropic Economic Index to assess exposure levels, based on the proportion of job tasks actually completed using AI tools.

Looking at specific occupations, computer programmers saw a real wage decline of 6.1%, statistical assistants of 5.4%, software quality analysts of 2.9%, and database architects of 2.7%—these traditionally high-skill positions have also not escaped the downward pressure on wages brought by AI. The white paper estimates that about 5.8 million workers in the U.S. are employed in jobs with high AI exposure, and this number is likely to rise sharply as AI accelerates its penetration into the business world.

Certainly, there is another side to the coin. Personal financial advisors may have over one-third of their tasks affected by AI, yet their wages increased by 8.4%; administrative law judges have about 30% of their tasks within the reach of AI, and their wages rose by 17.5% during the same period. This suggests that the impact of AI on wages is not uniform; some professions have actually seen increased output value due to AI assistance. However, for most high-exposure jobs, AI brings not the fear of job loss, but a more subtle erosion—you still have a job, but the leverage for a raise is quietly shrinking. This might be the most realistic narrative unfolding in the labor market in the AI era.

content_html_zh:
阿波罗全球管理公司发布的新白皮书提出了一个违反直觉的结论：人工智能可能不会直接抢走人们的工作，但它可能会首先压低工资。 一项跟踪 321 个职业的工资和就业数据的研究显示，自 2023 年以来（大致与 ChatGPT 的快速崛起同时），人工智能暴露程度最高的工作的平均工资增长率下降了 6.7%。

该研究尚未发现人工智能对整体就业产生“可察觉”的影响，这意味着更多的人目前面临的是加薪困难的现实，而不是失业的焦虑。

低收入群体首当其冲，程序员也未能幸免

工资影响的分布极不均匀。 2023年以来，服务业从业人员收入增速平均下降24.3%，底层25%人群收入下降10.7%，而最高收入群体并未受到“重大影响”。 研究人员还根据使用人工智能工具实际完成的工作任务的比例，使用人类经济指数来评估暴露水平。

从具体职业来看，计算机程序员的实际工资下降了6.1%，统计助理下降了5.4%，软件质量分析师下降了2.9%，数据库架构师下降了2.7%——这些传统的高技能岗位也没有逃脱人工智能带来的工资下降压力。 白皮书估计，美国约有 580 万工人从事人工智能暴露程度较高的工作，随着人工智能加速渗透到商业世界，这一数字可能会大幅上升。

当然，硬币还有另一面。 个人理财顾问可能有超过三分之一的工作受到人工智能的影响，但他们的工资却增加了8.4%；行政法法官约有30%的任务由人工智能完成，同期他们的工资上涨了17.5%。 这表明人工智能对工资的影响并不均匀；由于人工智能的帮助，一些行业的产值实际上有所增加。 然而，对于大多数高风险工作来说，人工智能带来的并不是失业的恐惧，而是一种更微妙的侵蚀——你仍然有工作，但加薪的杠杆却在悄然缩小。 这可能是人工智能时代劳动力市场上最现实的叙述。
